item.title: Demystifying the Red Zone: Optimizing Leaf Functions
item.description: Recently I’ve been learning Assembly language. Specifically focused on x86-64, using the GNU Assembler (GAS), in Intel syntax. I guess it’s my way of rebelling against AI: the higher-level they try to take me, the deeper down the stack I dive. If I get pushed any further, I will have no choice but to learn machine code. TL;DR: The Red Zone is a 128-byte region just below the stack pointer that the System V ABI guarantees won’t be clobbered by asynchronous kernel writes (like signal frames). This lets leaf functions skip stack-pointer bookkeeping. In this post I show the optimization in compiled output, then prove the guarantee empirically by triggering a signal and watching which stack bytes survive.
